Vey:
Vey is the central river country: broad cultivated flats, crowded landing towns, and older masonry exposed whenever banks retreat. Its upper water arrives from the chalk uplands; downstream channels eventually enter Orun. Freshwater kitchens and estuary-facing courts inhabit the same river without sharing one jurisdiction.

Travel here is usually easier by boat than by road, but recognized access matters as much as the vessel. A landing may accept a cargo and refuse its unregistered passenger. Kitchens, copying yards, and repair crews provide alternate evidence of a person’s actual life. Most settlements smell of grain steam, damp lime, lamp oil, and river mud rather than permanent incense.

The First Reckoning began among Vey’s witness cities. Their importance did not make them a universal sovereign. Later capitals repeatedly borrowed the common calendar to advertise a continuity their actual undertakings did not establish. The Bridge of Mercies and the Third Bowl preserve finite intervals of protection within that larger uncertainty.

In 1248, Vey faces stressed food routes and a struggle over whose testimony can revise inherited claims. Begin with the public kitchen histories for daily life, the painted quarter for kinship and civic representation, or Vesh’s inquiries for the morally difficult work of recovering an identity.
Orun:
Orun is the low reed country through which the basin reaches its eastern waters. Banks move, salt advances unevenly, and maps often name places no longer above water. Houses use raised floors, shallow craft, woven shade, and channels whose maintenance follows actual current more slowly than legal boundaries change.

Fragrant moth reed, grain, fish, and boat labor sustain its towns. Their prosperity is inseparable from food imported or carried between plots with very different fertility. Reed cultivation can protect a household from one danger and make it dependent upon another. The Green Tithe is the clearest example: rescue became an authentic limited claim surrounded by far larger human exactions.

Ordinary expertise lives in canal crews and kitchens as well as courts. A masked maintenance assembly records speakers’ responsibility while reducing immediate intimidation. A ferry boycott reveals how access can be unequal even when passengers pay equal prices. Blue water stations make care legible without promising free light or limitless clean water.

For travelers, a shallow route is not necessarily safe and an ancestral seal is not necessarily honest. In 1248 the practical question is which finite crossings, repairs, and food commitments can be sustained while wider disputes remain open. Heret Ford is a useful beginning because its military fame and everyday working geography continually contradict one another.
Keth:
Keth occupies the chalk uplands, where water disappears into fissures unless roofs and plastered channels catch it. Cistern chambers, burial niches, storage rooms, and classrooms compete for sheltered space. The pale landscape is marked by soot-dark work yards, colored glazes, patched lime, and ropes polished by repeated hauling.

Its early empire vanished, while weaving schools and many local undertakings continued. Successor rulers borrowed ancient names and impressive titles without automatically inheriting every right they advertised. The First Reckoning’s records and later consent rules give residents ways to inspect those claims.

Keth contains some of the basin’s clearest uncanny effects. Doubly held people experience divided movement beside incompatible obligations. Several basins take repeatable depths. A doorway returns every person to the approach while dry objects remain visibly beyond it. A bronze-bell descent reached drowned masonry but established no royal title to the chamber.

These phenomena coexist with ordinary leaks, damaged supports, bad ventilation, and fraud. Competent custodians inspect all of them without assuming one explanation must govern every case. In 1248, temporary refuge at unrelated springs protects affected people while slower inquiries proceed. Begin with the Crown of Peeled Stone for evidence and coercion, or the doorway and bell records for a mystery whose costs are known more clearly than its origin.
Talassar:
Talassar lies along the western salt marshes and sheltered boat country, with orchards and commercial towns linked to the wider basin through working vessels and negotiated routes. Tides regulate labor. Salt, oil, fragrant bark, repairing timber, and the custody of claims travel together. The appearance of durable family wealth often rests on distant households’ seasonal work.

Counting houses hold grain tallies, but an authentic tally proves only its actual scope. The Salt Heirs’ original tenth is not the same thing as every later labor demand imposed in its name. A harbor purchase can possess two credible records and two incompatible understandings. Its two bowls produce a bounded, costly overlap rather than declaring which ancestry is morally superior.

Taverns, murals, and public readers preserve versions of life absent from ceremonial commerce. Their independence requires roofs, meals, and small contributions. Pleasant harbor color therefore belongs to a maintenance history rather than an untouched golden age.

The recent mint earthquake exposed how coins and account entries differ from accessible food and safe shelter. In 1248, restoration faces old debts, damaged routes, and useful institutions whose authority needs inspection. Begin with the missing tenants and drowned room for commerce’s compromises, the empty-cloth negotiations for public accountability, or the purchased harbor for a dispute that can end only through executable terms.
Namar:
Namar’s passes join upland pasture to southern garden and caravan markets. A line across a map cannot describe the food, rest, shelter, and animal care a journey requires. Snow, exposed slopes, and seasonal grazing make the safest route change. Felt, leather, dried milk, stone, and packed seed portions provide the material palette of ordinary travel.

Hospices preserve obligations made by people who never returned. Those duties can support genuine welcome and create impossible costs when later patrons expand them. Pack crews, restraint teachers, and translators carry practical knowledge across jurisdictions that insist publicly on complete separation.

Its histories include a dynastic feast and disputed mountain crossing, divided provincial names, a caravan capital stranded by retreating water, and a strategic neck that changed toll authority without losing its repair needs. Pasture kingdoms formed through migration and intermarriage rather than one immaculate origin.

In 1248, the Blue Tile Convoy waits at a hospice while carriers negotiate food and finite repair work. That small delay illustrates the region better than a triumphant procession would. Begin with Ulven’s held-breath school for identity and movement, the milk cooperative for care and dependency, or the caravan neck for the difficult distinction between independence and useful continuing service.
Istren:
Istren is a rainy northern coast of fishing villages, timber houses, smoke yards, and small monasteries. Roof repair is a continuing trade. Boats connect settlements when paths become mud. Beyond the inhabited coast, the White Reach demands carefully maintained depots, dried food, and realistic return plans.

Its rulers once staged wrestling as evidence of unity and leased forest resin to outside merchants. Those histories remain visible in ordinary dependencies: hulls need sealing, shelters need beams, and crews need recognition that cannot be supplied through a spectacular victory image alone. Seasonal truces protect named work but must be revised when they overlook fishers, night labor, or winter conditions.

Collected songs and precise dance preserve testimony while remaining performances rather than unmediated historical proof. The care wards supply another difficult inheritance: useful institutions survived a patron whose reputation concealed harm. Residents need continuing provision and independent access, not merely a replacement monument.

In 1248, northern exploration competes with less prestigious depot maintenance for funds. Begin with the Cold River histories for the cost of bad preparation, the Locked Wards for institutional custody, or the White Reach logs for a journey whose safe return matters more than the solitary moment of first arrival.
Suth:
Suth’s southern inland valleys cultivate grafted orchards and carefully scheduled irrigation. Rootstocks, soil, water minerals, labor, and weather determine what grows. Star diagrams and prestigious cultivar names cannot replace that knowledge. Garden walls carry repairs from successive households, and their beauty often conceals precise practical work.

Asylum customs recognize strangers temporarily without automatically conveying every inherited right. Walking judges reduce travel costs while exposing exclusions within elected self-government. Protected meeting gardens remain inhabited productive places, not empty scenery made neutral by a ruler’s announcement.

The burial terraces preserve rulers, gardeners, lost communities, and stone reused from destroyed channels. Relay songs carry names through a landscape whose official inscriptions omitted them. Elsewhere, handcraft sweet workshops and a boarding school show useful generosity entangled with paternal authority.

In 1248, the Last Season practice offers a narrow substitute where a household’s intended recipient has vanished after careful inquiry. It cannot invent ownership of every unresolved ruin. Begin with the terrace repertoire for memory, the Peace Garden for finite cooperation, or the sweetmaking town for everyday pleasure whose food, fuel, and care remain accountable to real material limits.
Avel:
Avel’s islands lie off the drowned eastern coast, where low tides expose foundations and competing versions of early treaties. There is no single island people with one unchanged law. Sail crews, fishing households, shrine keepers, immigrants, and charter courts share sea passages while defending different rights.

The islands preserve the Mother of the Kept Breath as a tradition of finite hospitality. Their practical histories are less gentle: patron partitions, an imposed annexation’s distant consequences, rescued settlers excluding earlier hosts, and a sanctuary charter describing inhabited gardens as empty. Recognition of those costs need not erase genuine refuge or useful independence.

Observers compare stars from shaded orchards; musicians translate agreements into several landing tongues; a ball-casting school carries teaching across political boundaries. These practices demonstrate cooperation without proving that everyone has endorsed one territorial account.

The Southern Gate survived its recent siege by reopening water at a neighboring spring’s expense. Its wordless song is meaningful and cannot authenticate unstated charter terms. In 1248, amendment hearings connect performance, care evidence, representation, and compensation. Begin with the borrowed refuge for rescue’s complicated legacy, the unequal stars for inquiry misused as destiny, or the southern bell for remembrance that leaves room for present objections.
